content: The Asteraceae family, also known as Compositae, is commonly referred to as the aster, daisy, or sunflower family. It is an exceptionally large and widely distributed family of flowering plants (angiosperms). This family comprises approximately 33,000 currently recognized species, organized into 1,620 genera and 12 subfamilies. In terms of species diversity, Asteraceae is rivaled only by the Orchidaceae family. However, it remains unclear which of the two families is larger due to uncertainties regarding the exact number of species in each. The name Asteraceae is derived from the genus Aster, one of the most prominent genera in the family. The term Aster originates from the Greek word ἀστήρ (astēr), meaning star, which reflects the star-like appearance of the inflorescence in many species. The alternative name Compositae, though older, is still valid and refers to the composite nature of the flowers, a defining characteristic of this family. Asteraceae holds significant ecological and economic importance. It is found in a wide range of habitats, from polar regions to tropical zones, and has successfully colonized nearly all available ecosystems. In many regions, members of the Asteraceae family can constitute up to 10% of the native flora. The family is particularly abundant in arid and semi-arid regions of subtropical and lower temperate latitudes. The largest genera within the Asteraceae family include Senecio (1,000 species), Vernonia (1,000 species), Centaurea (700 species), Cousinia (600 species), Helichrysum (550 species), and Artemisia (550 species). While most members of the family are herbaceous plants, a significant number are shrubs, vines, or trees. Economically, Asteraceae is a highly valuable family. Several species provide products such as cooking oils, lettuce, sunflower seeds, artichokes, sweetening agents, coffee substitutes, and teas. Many genera are also popular in horticulture, including marigolds, pot marigolds (Calendula), coneflowers, various daisies, fleabanes (Erigeron), chrysanthemums, dahlias, zinnias, and heleniums. In herbal medicine, Asteraceae plays a crucial role, with species such as Grindelia, Echinacea, Achillea (yarrow), and many others being widely used for their medicinal properties. However, some members of the family have become invasive weeds. One notable example in North America is the dandelion (Taraxacum officinale), which is now widespread and well-known.
